readings.title: Red-winged Blackbird — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Weigh a writer’s praise of a bird against the complaints she reports.
readings.focus: A sociable marsh bird makes the best of life, while some farmers grumble about it.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. Oozy means soft and muddy; a bog or marsh is wet, spongy ground; grubs and cut-worms are young insects that harm crops; a brood is one family of eggs or chicks. The verse at the end is by the American poet Ralph Waldo Emerson.

excerpt.locator: Red-winged Blackbird entry, the narrative paragraphs and closing verse; opens “In oozy pastures where a brook lazily finds its way through the farm is the ideal…”; closes “—Emerson.”.

questions.prompt: How does Blanchan spell out the red-wing’s song? Try saying it, going up in pitch.
facilitatorNotes: “h’-wa-ker-ee” or “con-quer-ee,” rising up the scale. Writers spell bird songs as words to help readers hear them; Emerson’s verse spells it “O-ka-lee!”
evidence: "h'-wa-ker-ee" or "con-quer-ee"
The red-wing flutes his 'O-ka-lee!'

questions.prompt: Blanchan calls this bird “an impressive and helpful example of how to get the best out of life.” What does it do to earn that praise?
facilitatorNotes: It enjoys heat or cold, a big flock or a quiet treetop, and is satisfied with many kinds of food. It is easy to please wherever it is.
evidence: an impressive and helpful example of how to get the best out of life

questions.prompt: Why do some farmers dislike the blackbird, and how does Blanchan answer them?
facilitatorNotes: They complain of the noise and of the birds eating their corn. She answers that the birds ate grubs from that corn all summer, and that most of their food is weed-seeds or harmful insects. Ask whether her answer is fair to the farmers.
evidence: some farmers complain that the blackbird is the greatest nuisance
nearly seven-eighths of the redwing's food is made up of weed-seeds or of insects injurious to agriculture

questions.prompt: Blanchan says the birds “feel justly entitled to a share of the profits.” Can a bird really feel that? Why does she put it that way?
facilitatorNotes: She imagines the birds as workers owed their wages, a playful way of arguing for them. Children can separate what she saw (the birds eat grubs and corn) from what she imagined.
evidence: the birds feel justly entitled to a share of the profits

readings.title: Red-headed Woodpecker — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Separate what a writer saw from the comparisons and guesses she adds.
readings.focus: A loud, bright woodpecker digs its nest in shifts and stores nuts for later.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. Conspicuous means easy to see; plumage means feathers; a guttural sound comes from the throat; to excavate is to dig out; a milliner made ladies’ hats, which in Blanchan’s time were often trimmed with real birds’ feathers.
readings.contentNote: Blanchan mentions people shooting these birds and a snake eating the young in the nest.

excerpt.locator: Red-headed Woodpecker entry, the narrative paragraphs; opens “In thinly populated sections, where there are few guns about, this is still one of the…”; closes “…the young family, and that is a more deadly foe than even the sportsman or the milliner.”.

questions.prompt: What makes this woodpecker so easy to see and hear?
facilitatorNotes: Its glossy black-and-white body, its crimson head, a noisy rattle like a tree-toad’s, and its restless flitting from tree to tree.
evidence: its still more striking crimson head
ker-r-ruck, ker-r-ruck

questions.prompt: Blanchan says the woodpeckers’ red marks look as if they had been wounded there. Is that something she saw, or something she imagined?
facilitatorNotes: The red marks are real; the idea of a wound is her comparison. She also guesses that pressing against tree-trunks made them high-shouldered, which children may question.
evidence: as if they had been wounded there and bled a little

questions.prompt: How do the two parents share the work of digging the nest?
facilitatorNotes: They take turns. The one off duty gets “twenty minutes for refreshments” and comes back when its mate calls, as if the birds worked in shifts.
evidence: Both male and female take turns in this hollowing-out process.
twenty minutes for refreshments

questions.prompt: Which enemy does Blanchan call the most dangerous to this woodpecker?
facilitatorNotes: The black snake that gets into the nest, more deadly than hunters or hat-makers. Squirrels also help themselves to its stored nuts.
evidence: it is the black snake that enters the nest and eats the young family

readings.title: Chimney Swift — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Explain how a bird’s name fits what it does.
readings.focus: A fast, tireless flier lives inside people’s chimneys, which can be dangerous for it.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. In Blanchan’s day most houses were heated by fireplaces, and chimneys stood cold all summer. Nocturnal means active at night; a host is a crowd; woe betide means trouble will come to; embers are glowing coals.
readings.contentNote: Blanchan describes nests falling into a fire with the baby birds in them.

excerpt.locator: Chimney Swift entry, narrative paragraphs from “The chimney swift is, properly speaking” through the falling nests; opens “The chimney swift is, properly speaking, not a swallow at all, though chimney swallow is…”; closes “…rain also causes their nests to loosen their hold and fall with the soot to the bottom.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Blanchan say the swift is not really a swallow? What does it remind her of instead?
facilitatorNotes: Its stiff, rowing flight is unlike a swallow’s, and its whole look suggests a bat.
evidence: its entire aspect suggests a bat

questions.prompt: Blanchan says the name “chimney swift” is “everything it ought to be.” Explain both halves of the name.
facilitatorNotes: Swift: it flies powerfully, perhaps a thousand miles in a day. Chimney: it roosts and nests inside chimneys, clinging to the sides with its claws and tail.
evidence: the name of the chimney swift is everything it ought to be
sometimes covering a thousand miles in twenty-four hours

questions.prompt: What holds the swift’s nest to the chimney wall, and why does that matter later?
facilitatorNotes: The bird’s own saliva or tree-gum, used as glue. A fire melts it and heavy rain loosens it, so the nest can fall.
evidence: is glued with the bird's saliva or tree-gum into a solid structure
The glue being melted by the fire

questions.prompt: Which sounds and sights would tell a family that swifts live in their chimney?
facilitatorNotes: Twittering inside; a cloud of sooty birds wheeling above where smoke should be; a sound like distant thunder when they all whirl up at once.
evidence: What a twittering there is in the chimney
A sound as of distant thunder fills the chimney

readings.title: Kingbird — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Decide whether a name fits, using the writer’s evidence.
readings.focus: A bird named for a king turns out, in Blanchan’s eyes, to be a bully who avoids a fair fight.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. Pugnacious means eager to fight; provocation is a reason to start a fight; to show the white feather is to act like a coward; a drone is a male honey-bee; tyrant is part of the bird’s scientific name, Tyrannus.

excerpt.locator: Kingbird entry, the narrative paragraphs; opens “If the pugnacious propensity of the kingbird is the occasion of its royal name, he cannot…”; closes “…and takes his grand flights alone or with his queen, but never with a flock of his kind.”.

questions.prompt: Does Blanchan think the kingbird deserves to be called a king?
facilitatorNotes: No. She says it is named for its love of fighting, not for any noble quality: it is a born fighter “without provocation, rhyme, or reason.”
evidence: he cannot be said to deserve it from any fine or noble qualities he possesses

questions.prompt: How does the kingbird attack, and why does Blanchan call it unfair?
facilitatorNotes: It swoops on a bird in flight, strikes the head or neck and darts straight back to its perch, so it never receives a blow in return.
evidence: darting back like a flash to the exact spot from which he started
He never makes a fair hand-to-hand fight

questions.prompt: Which birds does the kingbird attack, and which does it run from or avoid?
facilitatorNotes: It attacks crows and hawks boldly and bullies small birds for fun; it turns tail when a small bird stands up to it and keeps well away from the catbird.
evidence: when the little victim shows pluck and faces his assailant, the kingbird will literally turn tail
he does not attempt to give battle to the catbird

questions.prompt: At the end Blanchan says the kingbird sits “in regal state on a conspicuous throne.” Is she praising him now?
facilitatorNotes: She is teasing him with royal words for a bird that keeps away from others of its kind. Some children hear the joke; others think she admires his independence.
evidence: sits in regal state on a conspicuous throne

readings.title: Phœbe — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice the questions a nature writer cannot answer, and what she has observed for certain.
readings.focus: The first flycatcher back each spring waits for its mate and then builds a nest close to people.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. Flycatchers are birds that catch insects in the air. Tardy means late; in embryo means not yet hatched or grown; a piazza is a porch; a rafter is a roof beam; a sally is a quick dash; to call something a song “by courtesy” is to call it that politely, more than it deserves.

excerpt.locator: Phœbe entry, narrative paragraphs from the March arrival through nest-building; opens “The earliest representative of the flycatcher family to come out of the tropics where…”; closes “…the wing, and with many a vivacious outburst of what by courtesy only we may name a song.”.

questions.prompt: What puzzles Blanchan about the phœbe’s return in March?
facilitatorNotes: What it can find to eat when the insects are not yet hatched, and why two birds mated for life do not travel north together. She admits these are mysteries.
evidence: what does the friendly little phœbe find to attract him to the north in March
is another of the many mysteries of bird-life awaiting solution

questions.prompt: How can you tell that Blanchan, or someone she trusts, has watched phœbes for many years?
facilitatorNotes: She knows the bird returns to the same place within a few days of the same date, year after year. That needs years of watching.
evidence: the date of his return will not vary by more than a few days in a given locality year after year

questions.prompt: What do the phœbes build their nest from, and where?
facilitatorNotes: Under a beam or rafter, with moss and mud for the base and hair, feathers or wool for the soft lining.
evidence: Presently a location is chosen under a beam or rafter
collecting moss and mud for the foundation and hair and feathers or wool to line the exquisite little home

questions.prompt: Blanchan says the phœbe’s song is a song only “by courtesy.” What does she think of it, and of the bird?
facilitatorNotes: The song is plain and repetitive, “pewit, phœbe,” but she enjoys the bird’s cheerful spirit as it works. Children may argue that a simple song is still a song.
evidence: contentedly but rather monotonously sing
what by courtesy only we may name a song

readings.title: Catbird — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a description that changes quickly, and picture each change.
readings.focus: A bird of opposite moods, elegant one moment and limp the next, sings beautifully and squawks like a cat.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde are two sides of one man in a famous story, one kind and one wicked; Beau Brummell was a famous dandy, a man very careful of his clothes. To prune and prink is to smooth and fuss over one’s looks; anon means soon after; a jester is a joker; epithets are names; depredations are raids.

excerpt.locator: Catbird entry, the narrative paragraphs; opens “Our familiar catbird, of all the feathered tribe, presents the most contrary…”; closes “…at all times and unusually adroit in catching insects, especially in the moth stage.”.

questions.prompt: Why is this bird called a catbird?
facilitatorNotes: Because of its harsh catcalls and squawks; Blanchan says that is where its common name comes from.
evidence: such harsh, altogether hateful catcalls and squawks as have given the bird his common name

questions.prompt: Blanchan shows the catbird changing its shape and mood. Choose two of its looks and act them out.
facilitatorNotes: An elegant dandy after its bath; a drooping, hang-dog bird; a limp little gray snake; a tense bird darting off into mischief. The quick changes are why she compares it to Jekyll and Hyde.
evidence: he appears from his toilet a Beau Brummell
till he looks like a little, short gray snake, lank and limp

questions.prompt: What is surprising about the catbird’s nest?
facilitatorNotes: Outside it is a “scrap-basket” of twigs, newspaper, scraps and rags; inside it is softly lined for the blue-green eggs.
evidence: The catbird's nest is like a veritable scrap-basket

questions.prompt: People call the catbird a fruit thief. Does Blanchan think it should be forgiven?
facilitatorNotes: Yes: it works hard and catches many insects, especially moths. Like her portrait of the blackbird, she weighs harm against good. Children can decide whether they agree.
evidence: surely his depredations may be pardoned
he is industrious at all times

readings.title: Junco — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how a nature writer uses other observers’ words alongside her own.
readings.focus: A shy gray winter visitor comes to the kitchen door when snow covers its food.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. Leaden means dull gray, like the metal lead; natty means neat and smart; vivacious means lively; to moult is to shed old feathers and grow new ones. Monks and nuns live in religious communities and often wore plain gray or brown robes. The snowflake here is a bird, now called the snow bunting.

excerpt.locator: Junco entry, the narrative paragraphs; opens “"Leaden skies above; snow below," is Mr. Parkhurst's suggestive description of this…”; closes “…trill, and a faint, whispered warble, usually much broken, but not without sweetness."”.

questions.prompt: When do juncos come close to houses, and why?
facilitatorNotes: When snow has buried the seeds and berries. Hunger makes these shy birds come to the kitchen door.
evidence: that is only starved into familiarity
When the snow has buried seed and berries

questions.prompt: Why might someone call juncos “little gray-robed monks and nuns”?
facilitatorNotes: Their plain gray backs look like robes, and they are neat and quiet and gather in groups.
evidence: little gray-robed monks and nuns

questions.prompt: How are juncos different from their sparrow cousins and from the snowflakes?
facilitatorNotes: They are not quarrelsome like sparrows, and although they like winter they hide from the worst storms, while snowflakes revel in them.
evidence: not quarrelsome, like their sparrow cousins
they nevertheless do not revel in the deep and fierce arctic blasts, as the snowflakes do

questions.prompt: Blanchan uses other bird-watchers’ words three times. Why do you think she does that?
facilitatorNotes: Parkhurst, Merriam and Bicknell each describe something well, and quoting them shows that several people have watched these birds. Some children may say she uses their words because they are better than hers.
evidence: as Miss Florence Merriam calls them
Mr. Bicknell describes it

readings.title: Belted Kingfisher — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Find the place where a writer feels sorry for a bird and laughs at it at the same time.
readings.focus: A noisy fisherman bird dives for its dinner, struggles to swallow it, and nests at the end of a tunnel.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. Secluded means hidden away; a sportsman’s fly is a fishing lure; conspicuous means easy to see; contortions are twistings; strident means harsh; to excavate is to dig; fledglings are young birds; to disgorge is to cough up.
readings.contentNote: The kingfisher kills a large fish by knocking it against a branch.

excerpt.locator: Belted Kingfisher entry, the narrative paragraphs; opens “If the kingfisher is not so neighborly as we could wish, or as he used to be, it is not…”; closes “…birds were being reared, hence the term "halcyon days," meaning days of fair weather.”.

questions.prompt: Why don’t kingfishers come close to our homes as they used to?
facilitatorNotes: The streams near houses have been fished out, so they must follow streams back to quiet ponds and lakes in the woods. It is not that they have grown less friendly.
evidence: because the streams near our homes are fished out

questions.prompt: Tell, step by step, how the kingfisher catches and eats a fish.
facilitatorNotes: It perches over the water and watches, drops and dives with a splash, returns with the fish in its beak, knocks a big fish against the branch, then gags and tries again and again to swallow it.
evidence: Suddenly the bird drops—dives; there is a splash, a struggle
A few sharp knocks, and the struggles of the fish are over

questions.prompt: Blanchan says the bird’s struggle to swallow makes us smile “in spite of the bird’s evident distress.” Is it all right to smile?
facilitatorNotes: It looks funny, and the writer admits that, while knowing the bird is uncomfortable. Some children will laugh; others will feel sorry for the bird. Both reactions are in the sentence.
evidence: force a smile in spite of the bird's evident distress

questions.prompt: What do a mated pair of kingfishers sound like, and how do they really feel?
facilitatorNotes: Their calls are harsh, rattling shrieks that sound like quarrelling, yet they are very devoted to each other.
evidence: It sounds as if they were perpetually quarrelling, and yet they are really particularly devoted.

questions.prompt: Where does the saying “halcyon days” come from?
facilitatorNotes: From old myths that the halcyon, or kingfisher, built a floating nest and calmed the sea while its young were hatched, so calm, fair days were named for it. Children may guess why people made up such a story about a bird of the water.
evidence: hence the term "halcyon days," meaning days of fair weather

readings.title: Blue Jay — a bird portrait (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Weigh what a writer says against a bird with what she says for it.
readings.focus: The beautiful blue jay is called many bad names, yet Blanchan would not want to lose it.
readings.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897; some of its facts and opinions about birds are out of date. To sojourn is to stay; reverence is deep respect; epithets are names; voracious means very greedy; plumage means feathers. Ralph Waldo Emerson was a famous American writer. A propensity is a habit; to pillage is to raid and rob; moulting is shedding old feathers.
readings.contentNote: Blue jays raid other birds’ nests and eat their eggs and young; the book judges the bird in moral words, such as “villainous,” that bird scientists would not use today.

excerpt.locator: Blue Jay entry, the narrative paragraphs; opens “No bird of finer color or presence sojourns with us the year round than the blue jay. In…”; closes “…not more than three or four true blue birds, and in England, it is said, there is none.”.

questions.prompt: What bad names have bird-watchers called the blue jay?
facilitatorNotes: Dishonest, cruel, inquisitive, murderous, voracious and villainous.
evidence: Dishonest, cruel, inquisitive, murderous, voracious, villainous

questions.prompt: What good does Emerson say the blue jay does?
facilitatorNotes: It buries nuts and hard seeds, so trees and shrubs grow in waste places; he says it does more good than harm.
evidence: he does "more good than harm,"

questions.prompt: Blanchan compares the jay to three other creatures. What are they, and what does each comparison mean?
facilitatorNotes: Mischievous as a small boy (full of tricks), destructive as a monkey (breaks and spoils things), and as good at hiding things as a squirrel (it buries nuts and seeds). Children may say which comparison fits best.
evidence: He is mischievous as a small boy, destructive as a monkey, deft at hiding as a squirrel.

questions.prompt: Why does Blanchan say we could “ill spare” the blue jay, even after all its faults?
facilitatorNotes: Its colour is like a bit of blue sky, and truly blue birds are rare. Beauty, she says, covers many sins.
evidence: like a bit of blue sky dropped from above
beauty covering a multitude of sins

questions.prompt: Is it fair to call a bird “villainous” for eating eggs? What do you think?
facilitatorNotes: Many children will say a jay eats eggs to live and cannot be wicked; others may feel sorry for the birds whose nests it robs. The book is old and judges birds the way people judge people.
evidence: to pillage and devour the young and eggs of their more peaceful neighbors
